## liboqs

### 0.17 essentials

At the last TSC meeting, the project set the goal of having all essential items for liboqs 0.17 merged by the next TSC meeting (November 24), so that the release process can start. All round 3 algorithms except FAEST have been merged, as has the deprecation of Classic McEliece. Four essential items on the prioritization board remain unmerged.

**FAEST ([PR #2592](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2592)).** Norm said the remaining review comments are small, and the PR mainly needs more reviewers. Sebastian Ramacher (FAEST team) approved it earlier in the day. It currently has merge conflicts, which keep reappearing as other PRs land. Norm committed to resolving them before November 20, the date Michael had proposed for having everything in. Douglas offered to block off a quiet day on `main` if that would make the rebase easier.

Michael agreed with Norm that a second review is what is missing, and said the rebase is straightforward. He had reviewed the PR closely and considers it good to go. However, some of the recent changes Norm brought in were copied from Michael's own branch, which he developed with Claude. Michael felt he should not be the one to approve work he had directed. Norm will add a note to the PR crediting the shared work from Michael and Claude, as Rodrigo had requested. Douglas did not see a problem: Norm has looked at Michael's contributions and Michael at Norm's, which gives two pairs of core team eyes, plus Sebastian's review. Michael then agreed to approve. As the PR would otherwise not have two approvals, he will override the requirement and merge once the conflicts are resolved.

(Note after the meeting: Michael approved PR #2592 during the meeting.)

**HQC update ([PR #2692](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2692)).** Bruce said the bulk of the work is done. Both the update to the v5.1 specification and the x86-optimized backends are in the PR. Since FAEST is more complex and has more moving parts, he is happy to queue up behind it, then rebase, resolve conflicts, and merge.

**SLH-DSA update.** In the meeting this was referred to as PR 2537; the PR described matches [PR #2587](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2587). Bruce, who has looked at it most closely, said it is a straightforward bump of the pinned upstream commit to one that fixes a memory-safety issue, the subject of a security advisory reported separately. He has approved it. A second review would be appreciated, but the PR is simple enough to merge after that. Douglas wondered whether it overlaps with Owen's recent [PR #2709](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2709) (for [issue #2686](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2686)), and apologized to Owen in case he had pointed him down the wrong track. Owen said his PR just bumps the commit hash to the latest upstream `main` and reruns `copy_from_upstream`. If PR #2587 is more involved or addresses a specific advisory, he would close his in favour of it. Bruce, Douglas and Owen will agree on which PR to proceed with. Both pin the same upstream repository, possibly at different commits.

(Note after the meeting: PR #2587 pins `slhdsa-c@d25ccc6` and adds a regression test for short signatures in `tests/test_sig.c`. PR #2709 pins a newer commit, `slhdsa-c@4745143`, which appears to include the same signature-length check, but does not add the test.)

**Merge order.** Norm will resolve the FAEST conflicts by the end of his day today. If Michael sees CI green when he gets to his office tomorrow (November 18), he will merge FAEST. He will then hand over to the Waterloo team to merge HQC and SLH-DSA, sequencing these among themselves.

### Non-essential PRs and release timeline

Rodrigo asked where to draw the line for PRs that are not on the essential list. Given the tight timeline, he would not add anything else, and nobody raised any other PR as needing to be in 0.17. Douglas suggested simply setting a deadline: any PR that gets over the line by then is in. Michael asked that the timeline he had proposed be published somewhere visible. Rodrigo found it in Michael's comment on the draft TSC agenda ([PR #364](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/pull/364)):

- November 20: feature freeze in liboqs
- November 24: first liboqs release candidate
- November 27: first release candidates for the subprojects to be released, at least oqs-provider
- December 4: liboqs RC2 if needed, otherwise finalization
- December 11: subproject RC2s or finalization
- December 18: final release opportunity for the year

Agreed: PRs for liboqs and oqs-provider close at the TSC meeting on November 24. The release candidate process then starts for liboqs, then oqs-provider, and hopefully the language wrappers.

### Upstream maintenance status ([issue #2678](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2678))

Michael would like a clean slate on the documented upstream maintenance status before the release, so that the release gives users a clear and honest statement of how each algorithm is supported. The case that prompted the issue was XMSS. LMS is documented as Cisco upstream with best-effort maintenance, which is fine. XMSS is documented as actively maintained, but the upstream XMSS reference repository has had no activity for five years. Michael had clicked through the other entries and saw nothing else glaringly wrong.

Douglas offered to contact Andreas Hülsing, the last committer and lead on the XMSS repository. Michael would welcome that; otherwise he is fine with simply stating "best effort". Rodrigo noted that the status levels formally describe the commitment upstream gives to working with OQS on reported vulnerabilities, not activity on the repository, though he agreed the two are correlated.

Rodrigo has been asking the upstream teams of the new algorithms for their commitment levels, but has not heard back from all of them. He will ask again this week, but missing answers will not block 0.17. Michael agreed, provided such entries are marked TBD so that users know there is no statement.

### Deprecating standardized algorithms ([issue #821](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/821), [PR #870](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/870))

Rodrigo raised the proposal to announce in oqs-provider 0.13.0 that the standardized algorithms will be removed in 0.14.0. If agreed, the deprecation notice has to go into the 0.13.0 release notes. The current text of the notice in PR #870 covers the ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA families "together with their standardized hybrid combinations (such as X25519MLKEM768) – all readily available from the OpenSSL default provider".

Douglas thought this is tied to the still-unresolved question of whether to split out hybrids ([issue #847](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/847), [PR #855](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/855)). Rodrigo disagreed. He reads #821 as dropping only what OpenSSL itself provides: the pure standardized algorithms and the three standardized hybrids. Other hybrids that involve a standardized algorithm would remain. Michael said he deliberately worded #821 so that it can be read either way, so the hybrid discussion can stay separate. In his view, it is not technically ideal to keep the other hybrids, since the provider must then carry all the code for the standardized algorithms. However, the question goes away if hybrids are split out. He thinks PR #870 can be approved as is, with the hybrid question tackled next, ideally also before the release.

Douglas said the point of the notice is to tell users that this release is the last to support something. Users should come away knowing exactly what is being removed and be able to act on it, for example from a list of the affected code points, rather than the text merely being consistent with whatever is later removed. Michael agreed that listing every algorithm and code point is possible. He said that on rereading, the notice matches Rodrigo's reading, and the term is well defined: exactly the algorithms readily available from the OpenSSL default provider. Douglas confirmed his understanding: a hybrid of ML-KEM with an elliptic curve not present in plain OpenSSL would continue to be supported after this release (unless hybrids are split out).

Norm asked about the ramifications, for example whether OQS could still create a hybrid of a new KEM with ML-KEM. Rodrigo said yes. OQS is free to create whatever hybrids it wants, and would only drop a combination once OpenSSL itself implements it. The PQ part of any hybrid in the provider always comes from liboqs, as the provider has no mechanism to choose another implementation. Nothing about this affects liboqs, which keeps ML-KEM.

Rodrigo summarized the practical effect. The provider already defers to OpenSSL for these algorithms on OpenSSL versions that include them. With 0.14.0, the provider would no longer offer them on older OpenSSL versions either. Users of OpenSSL 3.4 or earlier would then have no support for the standardized algorithms through oqs-provider, unless they stay on an earlier release. He noted that, with OpenSSL itself having recently ended support for 3.0, this could also be seen as dropping support for older OpenSSL versions.

No decision was taken. A collective decision is needed for the release, ideally by next week, and this will be part of the provider discussion at the TSC meeting. Rodrigo asked everyone to comment on the issue and to look at the other items on the provider prioritization board beforehand.

> **Action (all):** Comment on [issue #821](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/821) / [PR #870](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/870) and the provider prioritization board before the TSC meeting on November 24.

## oqs-demos

Dean was not present. Rodrigo suggested discussing demos governance at next week's TSC meeting, since Michael has raised legitimate concerns about how to handle it and demos are more complicated than the wrappers.

Aryan asked what the overall goal of the demos repository is. Rodrigo said the demos integrate post-quantum cryptography into well-known products, to show its impact and support its adoption. He expects the demos to play an important role in some upcoming events. Michael said the demos serve two purposes:

- They help get people involved, as a high-level way into the project and into integrating PQ algorithms in general.
- They act as canaries. The integrations used to be the first to flag a problem in oqs-provider or liboqs, such as a name change or a collision. They have not served this purpose well recently, since not enough time has gone into them.

Michael welcomed Aryan's PR ([PR #407](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-demos/pull/407), for [issue #406](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-demos/issues/406)) as a return to this mode of operation. Automatically creating an issue that explains why and where an integration fails would surface problems early, not only at integration or release time.
